title: Evaluation of the Impact of Design Parameters on the Acoustic Environment Perceived by Primary Students
research_question: To identify how architectural parameters of different learning spaces influence the acoustic environment perceived by primary students.

participants.description: Primary students aged 8-11 years old from 19 learning spaces across 9 primary schools in two cities in Chile (Santiago and Concepción). The sample was 59.0% female, 38.7% male, and 2.3% non-binary, with 98.0% native Spanish speakers.
participants.recruitment: Parents were sent consent letters from school managers. Students without permission were given an alternative activity or removed from class.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 19 learning spaces (classrooms) in 9 primary schools, categorized into four groups: Traditional learning space without acoustic treatment (TLE.NA, n=5), Traditional learning space with acoustic treatment (TLE.AA, n=3), Flexible learning space without acoustic treatment (FLE.NA, n=9), and Flexible learning space with acoustic treatment (FLE.AA, n=2). Spaces were characterized by geometry (height, floor size, volume), acoustic conditioning (percentage of sound-absorbing material, percentage of glass), window material, proximity to urban noise sources, and measured background noise level (Ln, dBA). Flexible design parameters included spatial density (m²/student), number of learning zones, diversity of furniture, and space adaptability.

mechanisms: Acoustic treatment (sound-absorbing materials) reduces reverberation and noise levels, leading to improved acoustic comfort and reduced annoyance.

Spatial density influences noise levels and perception, with higher density potentially leading to lower noise levels (as indicated by negative correlation between spatial density and Ln dBA in Table 7).
moderators: Type of learning space (traditional vs. flexible)
implementation_implications: Architectural design and acoustic conditioning are important for optimizing the acoustic experience in educational spaces.
Properly considering and managing background noise is crucial, especially since measured levels often exceed recommended thresholds.
Architectural design should align with contemporary educational needs to provide acoustic comfort and support dynamic pedagogical approaches.
Flexible spaces with acoustic treatment are associated with improved acoustic comfort, less noise annoyance, and enhanced hearing abilities.

limitations: The small number of learning spaces with acoustic treatment, due to the absence of regulatory requirements in Chile and schools' willingness to participate, means conclusions regarding the impact of design parameters on acoustic perception are tentative.
The questionnaire was completed by children aged 8-11 years old, who may have faced post-COVID-19 challenges in reading comprehension, potentially introducing bias despite teacher assistance.
Occupant noise levels were measured only during the survey procedure; measuring noise during lessons in different scenarios (e.g., presentation, group work) could provide more accurate conclusions.

paper_metadata.title: Multiple representations of the body schema for the same body part
paper_metadata.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

paper_metadata.crossref_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Significance
                  Accurate motor control depends on maps of the body in the brain, called the body schema. Disorders of the body schema cause motor deficits. Although we often execute actions with different motor systems such as the eye and hand, how the body schema operates during such actions is unknown. In this study, participants simultaneously directed eye and hand movements to the same body part. These two movements were found to be guided by different body maps. This finding demonstrates multiple motor system–specific representations of the body schema, suggesting that the choice of motor system toward one’s body can determine which of the brain’s body maps is observed. This may offer a new way to visualize patients’ body schema.
